transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um… I guess I’m here because this elevator thing has started getting a little out of hand. I mean, I can work around it most of the time, but I’ve realized I’m kind of planning my days around not having to use them.

Like, I’ll take five flights of stairs at home, and I turned down a workshop because it was in a high-rise. I’ve also stopped visiting one of my older computer students because his building doesn’t really have another option. That sounds bad when I say it out loud, but… yeah, that’s why I thought I should come in.
Is it just elevators that cause you anxiety, or are there other enclosed or high places that bother you as well?

Mostly elevators, I think. I don’t want to make it sound bigger than it is, because I know, like, an elevator in an office building is probably safe.

But when I see the older doors in my apartment building, or sometimes at work, my brain just kind of jumps to, “What if I get trapped?” or “What if it drops?” Even saying that sounds a bit dramatic, I know. It’s more that my mind reacts like it’s about to happen, even though part of me knows that’s not really reasonable.
Have you ever felt anxious or uncomfortable in other small or enclosed spaces, like cars or tunnels?

Not really cars or tunnels, no… at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more elevators specifically.

I know, like, an elevator in an office block is probably safe, so I don’t want to sound irrational. But when I’m looking at the older doors in my apartment building, or sometimes at work, my mind just treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there or it’s going to drop. Part of me knows that sounds over the top, but that’s where my head goes.
Have you started avoiding other activities or places because of your concerns about elevators?

Yeah… a few, I guess. I don’t want to make it sound like I never leave the house or anything, because I do. But I have started sort of arranging things around avoiding elevators.

Like at home I’ll take the stairs even though it’s five flights, and I turned down a workshop because it was in a high-rise building. And… I’ve stopped visiting one of the older people I help with computer lessons because his building doesn’t really have another easy option besides the elevator. That one makes me feel a bit bad, honestly.
Have you ever had a sudden, intense feeling of fear or discomfort when you were in an elevator?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t want to call it some huge episode or anything, but yes. Sometimes it hits really suddenly.

Like as soon as I step toward the elevator, or even when I hear it clunk open, my chest kind of tightens and my hands get sweaty. There’s this rush of panic before I’ve even really had time to think about it. I know that probably sounds a bit much, but that’s what it feels like in the moment.
Is your fear of elevators related to being in a small, enclosed space or is it more about the fear of something happening to the elevator itself, like it falling?

I think it’s more about something happening to the elevator itself, if that makes sense. Like… I know an office elevator is probably safe, and I’m not trying to be dramatic, but when I see the older doors in my apartment building or sometimes at work, my mind goes straight to, “What if I get trapped?” or “What if it drops?”

So it’s not just the small space, exactly. It’s more that fear that the elevator won’t work properly, even though part of me knows that sounds kind of over the top.
Do you think your fear would decrease if you were in an elevator with someone you trust, like a friend or family member?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I think it might help a little, like I’d feel less embarrassed or less alone if someone I trusted was there. But I don’t know if it would really make the fear go away.

I haven’t paid super close attention to that specifically. I guess I’d still be thinking about the elevator itself, if that makes sense. But maybe having someone there would make it easier to get through. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Would your fear decrease if you were in control of the elevator, for example, if you were the one operating it?

I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think I’ve really been in a situation where I felt like I was “in control” of it, beyond just pressing the button for my floor.

Maybe it would help a little if I knew exactly what was happening, but… I don’t want to overstate it. I think I’d still be aware that it’s the elevator doing its own thing, you know? Does that answer it okay?
Is your fear of elevators more about the machinery and mechanics of the elevator itself, rather than just being in a small space?

Yeah, I think that’s probably closer to it. It’s not just that the space is small. I mean, I know logically an office elevator is probably safe, but when I see the older doors in my apartment building or even at work, my brain kind of jumps to, “What if I get trapped?” or “What if it drops?”

I know that probably sounds a little over the top, but that’s where my mind goes. Does that make sense?
Are there any other specific situations or objects, besides elevators, that trigger a similar fear of being trapped or something going wrong?

Not that I can really think of. I mean, I’m trying to think of anything else like that, but elevators are the main thing that comes to mind.

Maybe I get a little uncomfortable in some situations where I can’t just easily leave, but I don’t know if it’s the same kind of fear, and I don’t want to make it sound bigger than it is. Elevators are definitely the thing I’ve noticed most. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Is your fear of elevators ever triggered by thoughts of the elevator stopping or malfunctioning in any way, rather than just falling?

Yeah, I think so. It’s not only the idea of it falling. A lot of the time it’s more like, “What if it stops?” or “What if the doors don’t open and I’m stuck in there?”

I know, realistically, an office elevator is probably fine, and I don’t want to make it sound dramatic. But when I see the older doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind kind of treats it like something’s about to go wrong, like I’ll get trapped or it’ll drop. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you ever feel a similar sense of fear or panic in situations where you're not in an elevator but still feel trapped or unable to leave?

I don’t think so, not in the same way. I mean, maybe if I’m somewhere crowded or it’s hard to get out, I might feel a little uneasy, but I wouldn’t really call it panic.

It’s mostly elevators that bring that feeling up. I don’t want to overstate it, but that’s the one that really stands out to me. Does that make sense?
Do you think you would feel anxious or uncomfortable if you were in a small, enclosed space that was not an elevator, such as a small room without windows?

I’m not totally sure. I don’t think a small room without windows would bother me in the same way, as long as I knew I could open the door and leave.

I might feel a little uncomfortable if it felt really cramped, but I haven’t noticed that same fear like I get with elevators. It’s more the elevator itself and the idea of it getting stuck or not opening, if that makes sense.
Do you think you would feel anxious if you were in a situation where you felt trapped but had no relation to elevators, such as being in a traffic jam?

I don’t think so, not really. Like, traffic jams can be annoying, and I might get a little impatient, but I don’t usually feel that same trapped panic feeling.

I guess if it was extreme maybe I’d be uncomfortable, but day to day, no, it doesn’t seem to hit me the way elevators do. Is that the kind of distinction you’re asking about?
Would you feel anxious or uncomfortable in other situations where you have no control over your environment?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I don’t love not being in control of things, but I don’t think I usually get anxious just because of that.

If I’m in some situation where I can’t control what’s happening, I might feel a little tense or annoyed, but I haven’t really noticed it becoming a fear thing. At least not like with elevators. Is that an okay way to put it?
Would your fear of elevators decrease if you were using a freight elevator or a similar elevator that is not typically used by the general public and is usually on the ground level?

Maybe a little, if it felt more open or like it wasn’t really going anywhere. But I don’t think it would fully go away.

I know, logically, an elevator in an office building or something is probably safe. But when I see those older doors, like in my apartment building or at work, my brain kind of treats it like I’m about to get trapped or like it could drop, even though I know that probably sounds over the top.

So if it was a freight elevator on the ground level, I might tell myself it’s fine, but I think I’d still feel that anxiety come up. Does that answer it?
Would you feel anxious or uncomfortable in a similar enclosed space like a subway car or a train?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I’ve been on trains and subway cars before, and I don’t think I react the same way as with elevators.

They can feel crowded or uncomfortable sometimes, but I don’t know that I’d call it anxious in the same way. Maybe if it was really packed or stopped for a while I’d feel uneasy, but I haven’t really noticed it being a major issue. Is that helpful?
Would you feel anxious if you were in a similar enclosed space like a small, enclosed room that has the possibility of malfunctioning, such as an airlock?

Yeah, I think… maybe if it reminded me of an elevator in that way, I’d probably get anxious.

Like, I know an elevator in an office building is probably safe, but when I see those older doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind jumps to, “What if I get trapped?” or “What if it drops?” even though I know that probably sounds kind of dramatic.

So with something like that, if it had that same feeling of being enclosed and able to malfunction, I think my brain might react similarly. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Would you feel anxious in a small, enclosed space like a funicular or a cable car?

Maybe, yeah… I haven’t really been in those much, so I don’t want to overstate it.

But if it had that same feeling as an elevator—small, closed in, like I couldn’t just get out—then I think I’d probably feel anxious. It’s not that I think every one of those is actually dangerous. I know, like, an elevator in an office building is probably safe. But when I see old elevator doors at my apartment or work, my mind kind of goes straight to, “What if I get trapped?” or “What if it drops?” even though I know that sounds a bit over the top.

So with a cable car or funicular, if it triggered that same idea, I think I’d be uncomfortable. Is that the kind of answer you’re looking for?
